newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada fishermen continue blockade of U.S. ferry.
newsitem.headline: Canada fishermen continue blockade of U.S. ferry.

text.p: Defying a court order, angry Canadian fishermen maintained their blockade of an Alaska ferry on Monday as tensions rose between the United States and Canada over salmon fishing.

About 150 fishing boats surrounded the Alaska state ferry Malaspina for the third day in the harbor at Prince Rupert, British Columbia, 1,000 miles (1,600 km) north of Vancouver. About 142 passengers were aboard the ferry.
"The ferry is still under blockade. We're hopeful it will be able to go soon, but we just don't know," said Murray Sheppard, an official with the ferry line in Prince Rupert.
Canada has accused the United States of overfishing Pacific Ocean salmon while U.S. officials contend Canada is to blame for scuttling recent talks on a deal to divide this year's catch.
Canadian police were expected to begin on Monday enforcing a court order compelling the fishing boats to free the ferry, but it was still unclear when the ship might sail.

"They will have to serve an injunction on each boat. It could take all day and then some to clear the harbor," said John Cummins, a Canadian member of parliament from the Vancouver area who traveled to Prince Rupert.
Frustration has mounted in British Columbia fishing communities over recent days amid allegations that Alaskan fishermen have taken more than double their normal catch of salmon so far this year.

In Prince Rupert, a flotilla of fishing boats prevented the ferry from sailing on Saturday after it made a regular stop on its way from Seattle to Ketchikan, Alaska. Irate fishermen shouted obscenities and burned an American flag, Canadian media reported.
Acting on a request by Alaska, a Canadian federal court on Sunday ordered the fishermen to release the ship and there were negotiations with the fishermen through the night.
But the talks collapsed and the fishermen said Monday that pleasure boats and new fishing boats were joining the protest in an effort to prolong the process of ending the blockade.
"The blockade is growing," Jim Sinclair, an official with the United Fishermen and Allied Workers union in Prince Rupert. "...People are very upset."

Alaska has threatened to discontinue ferry service to Prince Rupert. "The passengers are just being used as pawns in this, which we think is totally wrong," Bob King, press secretary to Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles, said on Sunday.
Over the weekend, the ferry's 300 passengers got off and stayed at hotels in Prince Rupert. Some made other travel arrangements while others reboarded in hopes of continuing their trip.
The so-called Alaska Marine Highway is a lifeline for towns along Alaska's coast and is popular with tourists.

In Vancouver, British Columbia Premier Glen Clark was holding meetings on the situation with federal Fisheries Minister David Anderson and Defense Minister Art Eggleton. Anderson was due to fly to Prince Rupert later.
Clark sent an open letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton urging him to intervene and halt Alaskan fishing.

The dispute followed years of squabbling over salmon. Canada last week accused the United States of violating a treaty between the two countries by overfishing in Alaska, but the United States rejected the claim. Canada wants the two countries to submit the dispute to binding international arbitration.
